content: Hydrocortisone is a medication that can be obtained with or without a prescription. Over-the-counter formulations, such as 0.5% or 1% hydrocortisone, are used to temporarily relieve minor skin irritations, itching, and rashes caused by conditions like eczema, insect bites, poison ivy, poison oak, poison sumac, soaps, detergents, cosmetics, and jewelry. It is also used to alleviate itching in the anal and rectal areas, as well as itching and irritation of the scalp. Additionally, hydrocortisone can be applied to relieve discomfort from mouth sores. When prescribed by a doctor, hydrocortisone is used to manage itching, redness, dryness, crusting, scaling, inflammation, and discomfort associated with various skin conditions. It may also be prescribed to reduce inflammation in conditions like ulcerative colitis or proctitis, or to alleviate swelling and discomfort caused by hemorrhoids and other rectal issues. In some cases, hydrocortisone may be prescribed for other uses; consult your doctor or pharmacist for more information. Hydrocortisone is available in various forms, including ointments, creams, lotions, liquids, gels, medicated cloth towelettes, and sprays for skin application; foams, suppositories, creams, ointments, and enemas for rectal use; and pastes for use in the mouth. For skin conditions, it is typically applied one to four times daily. For mouth sores, it is usually applied two to three times daily after meals and at bedtime. If mouth sores do not begin to heal within seven days, contact your doctor. For colitis, hydrocortisone is generally used every night or twice daily (morning and night) for two to three weeks. While symptoms may improve within three to five days, regular enema use may be required for two to three months. If colitis symptoms do not improve within three weeks, consult your doctor. For proctitis, hydrocortisone is typically used once or twice daily for two to three weeks, and then, if necessary, every other day until the condition improves. Symptoms of proctitis may improve within five to seven days. For hemorrhoids, hydrocortisone is usually applied twice daily (morning and night) for two to six days. Follow the instructions on the medication label carefully, and ask your doctor or pharmacist if you have any questions. Use hydrocortisone exactly as directed. Do not use more or less of it, or use it more frequently than prescribed. If you obtained hydrocortisone without a prescription and your condition does not improve within seven days, stop using it and contact your doctor. Notify your doctor if any treated area worsens or if redness, swelling, or pus develops. To apply hydrocortisone ointment, cream, lotion, liquid, or gel to the skin, thoroughly wash or soak the affected area before application unless doing so irritates your skin. Apply a thin layer of the medication and rub it in gently. For scalp application, part your hair, apply a small amount of the medication to the affected area, and rub it in gently. Avoid washing or rubbing the area until the medication dries. You may wash your hair as usual, but not immediately after applying the medication. To use the aerosol spray, shake the container well and spray the affected area from a distance of 3–6 inches for about two seconds to cover an area the size of your hand. Avoid inhaling the vapors. If spraying near your face, cover your eyes. Avoid prolonged use on the face, genital and rectal areas, and skin folds or armpits unless directed by your doctor. If using hydrocortisone on your face, keep it away from your eyes. If applying it to a child’s diaper area, avoid tight-fitting diapers or plastic pants, as these may increase side effects. Do not apply cosmetics or other skin preparations to the treated area without consulting your doctor. If your doctor instructs you to wrap or bandage the treated area, follow these steps: 1. Soak or wash the area thoroughly. 2. While the skin is moist, gently rub the medication into the affected areas. 3. Cover the area with plastic wrap (e.g., Saran Wrap or Handi-Wrap). Secure the plastic with gauze, an elastic bandage, or adhesive tape on the normal skin surrounding the treated area. Alternatively, plastic gloves may be used for hands, plastic bags for feet, or a shower cap for the scalp. 4. Seal the edges of the plastic wrap carefully to ensure it adheres closely to the skin. If the area is moist, leave the edges partly unsealed or puncture the wrap to allow excess moisture to escape. 5. Leave the plastic wrap in place as directed by your doctor, usually no more than 12 hours per day. 6. Cleanse the skin and reapply the medication each time a new plastic wrapping is applied. For rectal cream or ointment, apply it externally to the anal area. Some nonprescription creams may be applied to the genital and anal areas; read the product label carefully. Hydrocortisone enemas come with specific instructions that should be followed closely. Lie on your left side while using the enema and for 30 minutes afterward. Try to retain the enema for at least one hour, preferably overnight. Rectal foam also comes with specific instructions and should be applied using the provided applicator. Do not insert any part of the container into your rectum. After using the applicator, disassemble it and clean it thoroughly with warm water. To insert a rectal suppository: 1. Remove the wrapper. If the suppository is too soft to insert, chill it in the refrigerator for 30 minutes or run cold water over it before removing the foil wrapper. 2. Dip the tip of the suppository in water. 3. Lie on your left side and raise your right knee to your chest. (Left-handed individuals should lie on their right side and raise their left knee.) 4. Using your finger, insert the suppository into the rectum (about 1/2 to 1 inch for infants and children, and 1 inch for adults). Hold it in place for a few moments. 5. Remain lying down for 15 minutes. Then, stand up, wash your hands thoroughly, and resume your normal activities. Note that some hydrocortisone suppositories may stain fabric, so take necessary precautions. Before using hydrocortisone, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to hydrocortisone or any other drugs. Provide a list of all prescription and nonprescription medications you are taking, especially cancer chemotherapy agents, other topical medications, and vitamins. Notify your doctor if you have an infection or a history of diabetes, glaucoma, circulation disorders, or immune disorders. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, inform your doctor. If you become pregnant while using hydrocortisone, contact your doctor immediately. Do not use hydrocortisone on children under two years of age without consulting a doctor. If you miss a dose, apply it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and continue your regular dosing schedule. Do not apply a double dose to make up for a missed one. Hydrocortisone may cause side effects. Notify your doctor if you experience any of the following symptoms and they are severe or persistent: Drying or cracking of the skin Acne Itching Burning Changes in skin color If you experience any of the following severe side effects, contact your doctor immediately: Severe skin rash Difficulty breathing or swallowing Wheezing Skin infection (redness, swelling, or pus) If you experience a serious side effect, you or your doctor may report it to the FDA’s MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program online or by phone. Store hydrocortisone in its original container, tightly closed, and out of reach of children. Follow the storage instructions on the package. Dispose of outdated or no longer needed medication properly. Consult your pharmacist for guidance on proper disposal. Keep all appointments with your doctor. Do not share your medication with others. If you have questions about refilling your prescription, consult your pharmacist.
